EDA¶

Dataset: UCI "Parking Birmingham" — car park occupancy readings collected across ~30 Birmingham lots, Oct–Dec 2016. 4 columns: SystemCodeNumber (lot ID), Capacity, Occupancy, LastUpdated (timestamp string).

Every lot's median gap clusters tightly around ~33 minutes, with almost no spread across lots. This consistency points to a shared polling schedule rather than independent per-lot sensor behavior.

Nearly all lots share the same :03 second offset in their timestamps — consistent with one centralized polling job. Three lots (BHMBRTARC01, BHMNCPLDH01, NIA North) show different offsets (:17, :22, :51), suggesting they were sourced from a separate collection pipeline. This doesn't change the resampling plan (all lots share the same ~33min cadence regardless of offset), but it's a useful data-provenance note, and these three lots turn out to be exactly the ones with poor coverage later.

Conclusion on resample frequency: the true intended polling interval is almost certainly a round 30 minutes — the observed 33min median is 30min plus a small systematic delay from the collection process (confirmed by the consistent :03-second offset). Resampling at 33min would bake this measurement artifact into the pipeline; resampling at 30min corrects for it and keeps a clean, round grid for downstream feature engineering.

Resampling to a Fixed 30-Minute Grid¶

Resample each lot independently onto a regular 30-min grid. This creates explicit NaN rows wherever no reading existed in a given window — intentional, so gaps are visible and handled deliberately rather than silently smoothed over.

In [20]:
# Make sure LastUpdated is the index (required for resample)
parking = parking.set_index('LastUpdated')

# Resample per lot onto a fixed 30-min grid
resampled = (
    parking.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')
      .resample('30min')
      .agg({'Occupancy': 'mean', 'Capacity': 'first'})
)

# Flatten the MultiIndex (SystemCodeNumber, LastUpdated) back into columns
resampled = resampled.reset_index()

Two clear patterns:

  • Weekends (Fri/Sat) show higher missingness (~43–46%) than mid-week (~32–37%) — a real characteristic of the data, not a boundary artifact.
  • A handful of lots are far worse than the rest: NIA North (87.5%) and BHMBRTARC01 (44%) stand out, and cross-referencing with the date-range check below shows they also have drastically shorter history (45 and 5 days respectively, vs. ~76 for most lots). These are the same lots flagged earlier as coming from a different collection pipeline. NIA North also accounts for the 12 negative Occupancy readings found in the raw data, reinforcing that it's an unreliable source rather than just a coverage gap.

Two other lots (NIA Car Parks, NIA South) also appeared near the top of the missingness list but have a full date range (~73 days, unlike the two above) — these are rechecked separately after dropping hour 7 to see whether their elevated missingness was a genuine issue or just an hour-7 artifact.

Decision: drop hour 7, then drop the two clearly unreliable lots (NIA North, BHMBRTARC01), and re-evaluate the rest.

Gap-Length Analysis & Interpolation¶

Before filling any missing values, measure how long individual gaps (consecutive missing streaks) actually are. Short gaps are safe to interpolate; long gaps should be left as genuine missing data rather than fabricated.

In [35]:
# work per lot, since gaps are lot-specific
resampled_clean = resampled_clean.sort_values(['SystemCodeNumber', 'LastUpdated'])

resampled_clean['is_missing'] = resampled_clean['Occupancy'].isna()

# identify consecutive missing streaks per lot
resampled_clean['gap_group'] = (
    resampled_clean.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['is_missing']
    .apply(lambda x: (x != x.shift()).cumsum())
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

gap_lengths = (
    resampled_clean[resampled_clean['is_missing']]
    .groupby(['SystemCodeNumber', 'gap_group'])
    .size()
)

Heavily right-skewed: ~95% of gap events are 4 steps (2 hours) or shorter, and gaps of length 1–2 alone account for ~59% of all missing rows. This supports capping interpolation at 4 steps — short gaps get a defensible linear fill, while the long tail (2.5+ hours) is left as real missing data rather than guessed at.

In [37]:

In [38]:
MAX_FILL_STEPS = 4

resampled_clean['Occupancy_filled'] = (
    resampled_clean.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['Occupancy']
    .transform(lambda x: x.interpolate(method='linear', limit=MAX_FILL_STEPS, limit_area='inside'))
)

resampled_clean['was_imputed'] = (
    resampled_clean['Occupancy'].isna() & resampled_clean['Occupancy_filled'].notna()
)

still_missing = resampled_clean['Occupancy_filled'].isna().sum()
total = len(resampled_clean)
print(f"Still missing after fill: {still_missing} / {total} ({still_missing/total:.1%})")
print(f"Rows imputed: {resampled_clean['was_imputed'].sum()}")

Still missing after fill: 2885 / 38700 (7.5%)
Rows imputed: 10034

Missingness reduced from 33.4% to 7.5% via capped linear interpolation (≤4 steps / 2 hours), with 10,034 rows filled and flagged via was_imputed. The remaining 7.5% (long gaps of 2.5+ hours) are dropped — filling them would fabricate multi-hour trends the data doesn't actually support.

Resampling created empty rows for every missing time slot, which also nulled out Capacity (a static per-lot value) in those rows. Forward/backward-fill it — safe since it's a known constant, not something being estimated.

In [39]:
resampled_clean['Capacity'] = (
    resampled_clean.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['Capacity']
    .transform(lambda x: x.ffill().bfill())
)

print(resampled_clean['Capacity'].isna().sum())  # should be 0

0
In [40]:

final_df = final_df.drop(columns=['gap_group', 'is_missing', 'Occupancy'])
final_df = final_df.rename(columns={'Occupancy_filled': 'Occupancy'})

Feature Engineering¶

Build the target variable and predictive features. First: normalize occupancy into a rate (0–1) so lots of different sizes are directly comparable — important since lots will later be pooled into a single model.

In [42]:
final_df['OccupancyRate'] = final_df['Occupancy'] / final_df['Capacity']
In [43]:
final_df['hour'] = final_df['LastUpdated'].dt.hour
final_df['dayofweek'] = final_df['LastUpdated'].dt.dayofweek      # 0=Monday
final_df['is_weekend'] = final_df['dayofweek'].isin([5, 6]).astype(int)
final_df['date'] = final_df['LastUpdated'].dt.date

Confirmed: observed peak occupancy modestly exceeds stated capacity for the three affected lots (e.g. BHMBCCTHL01: stated 387 vs. observed max 403). Fix by recomputing Capacity as max(stated, observed max) per lot — this corrects the denominator without touching the underlying Occupancy readings, which were accurate all along.

In [50]:
observed_max = final_df.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['Occupancy'].transform('max')
final_df['Capacity'] = final_df[['Capacity']].assign(obs=observed_max).max(axis=1)

# recompute the rate cleanly
final_df['OccupancyRate'] = final_df['Occupancy'] / final_df['Capacity']

print((final_df['OccupancyRate'] > 1).sum())  # should now be 0

0

Capacity corrected; no more rate-overshoot rows. This preserves genuine peak-demand signal for the affected lots instead of artificially clipping it.

Lag & Rolling Features (for pooled ML approach)¶

Since operating hours are 8:00–16:00 (18 slots/day at 30min resolution, not 24), lag windows are defined relative to this 18-slot day rather than a calendar day. Rolling means are shifted by 1 step first to avoid leaking the current value into its own feature.

In [56]:
final_df = final_df.sort_values(['SystemCodeNumber', 'LastUpdated'])

SLOTS_PER_DAY = 18  # 8:00–16:00 inclusive at 30min steps

# lags
final_df['lag_1step'] = final_df.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['OccupancyRate'].shift(1)
final_df['lag_2step'] = final_df.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['OccupancyRate'].shift(2)
final_df['lag_1day']  = final_df.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['OccupancyRate'].shift(SLOTS_PER_DAY)

# rolling mean (shift(1) first so you don't leak the current value)
final_df['roll_mean_4'] = (
    final_df.groupby('SystemCodeNumber')['OccupancyRate']
    .transform(lambda x: x.shift(1).rolling(4).mean())
)

Drop rows with NaN lags — these are the first few rows of each lot's series where there isn't enough history yet to compute lag/rolling features. This is the feature-complete table ready for the pooled model.

In [57]:
# lot identity as categorical
final_df['SystemCodeNumber'] = final_df['SystemCodeNumber'].astype('category')

# drop rows where lag/rolling features are NaN (start of each lot's series)
lag_roll_cols = ['lag_1step', 'lag_2step', 'lag_1day', 'roll_mean_4']
model_df = final_df.dropna(subset=lag_roll_cols).copy()

Train/Test Split¶

Sanity-check data coverage by week before picking a split boundary — want to avoid a test period that lands on a thin or partial week.

In [62]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

weekly_counts.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(12, 4), title='Entries per Week')
plt.ylabel('Row count')
plt.xlabel('Week')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
In [63]:
print(model_df['LastUpdated'].max())

2016-12-19 16:30:00

The final week (Dec 19–25) has drastically fewer rows (468 vs. ~3300+ typical). Checking the max timestamp confirms the dataset simply stops on Dec 19 — this isn't a partial day, it's an isolated single day with the rest of that week entirely absent from the data.

Given the isolated final day, use an explicit date range for the test set (Dec 5–18: two full weeks) rather than a naive "last 14 days" cutoff, which would otherwise pull in that disconnected single day and skew the test set.

In [64]:
cutoff = model_df['LastUpdated'].max() - pd.Timedelta(days=14)
print('Cutoff:', cutoff)

Cutoff: 2016-12-05 16:30:00

pooled_test_df  = model_df[model_df['LastUpdated'] >= cutoff].copy()

print(f"Test:  {pooled_test_df.shape}, {pooled_test_df['LastUpdated'].min()} to {pooled_test_df['LastUpdated'].max()}")

                 'lag_1step', 'lag_2step', 'lag_1day', 'roll_mean_4']

Feature set excludes LastUpdated, date (raw datetime — replaced by extracted hour/dayofweek/is_weekend), Occupancy (would leak the target directly via Occupancy/Capacity), and was_imputed (not knowable at genuine forecast time — kept in the dataframe for diagnostics only).

Baseline Result¶

Persistence forecast — predict "no change from 30 minutes ago" using lag_1step directly. No model, no fitting; this is the floor any real model needs to beat.

In [68]:
#pip install scikit-learn
In [69]:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
import numpy as np

# Baseline: "predict the last known value" (lag_1step itself)
baseline_pred = X_test['lag_1step']
baseline_mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, baseline_pred)
baseline_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, baseline_pred))
print(f"Baseline MAE: {baseline_mae:.4f}, RMSE: {baseline_rmse:.4f}")

Baseline MAE: 0.0479, RMSE: 0.0825

Pooled Model: LightGBM¶

Train a single model across all lots (with SystemCodeNumber as a categorical feature) rather than one model per lot — chosen given the moderate dataset size (~30K rows across 28 lots with ~2.5 months of history), where pooling lets the model borrow strength across lots' shared patterns.

In [70]:
#pip install lightgbm
In [71]:
import lightgbm as lgb

train_set = lgb.Dataset(X_train, label=y_train, categorical_feature=['SystemCodeNumber'])
test_set = lgb.Dataset(X_test, label=y_test, categorical_feature=['SystemCodeNumber'], reference=train_set)

params = {
    'objective': 'regression',
    'metric': 'mae',
    'learning_rate': 0.05,
    'num_leaves': 31,          # default; start here, don't overtune yet
    'min_data_in_leaf': 50,    # guards against overfitting on a moderate-size dataset
    'feature_fraction': 0.9,
    'bagging_fraction': 0.8,
    'bagging_freq': 5,
    'verbose': -1,
}

model = lgb.train(
    params,
    train_set,
    num_boost_round=1000,
    valid_sets=[test_set],
    callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(stopping_rounds=50), lgb.log_evaluation(period=100)]
)

preds = model.predict(X_test, num_iteration=model.best_iteration)
print(f"LightGBM MAE: {mean_absolute_error(y_test, preds):.4f}")
print(f"LightGBM RMSE: {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, preds)):.4f}")

Training until validation scores don't improve for 50 rounds

Pooled Model: XGBoost Training¶

Trying XGBoost as a second gradient-boosting model for comparison, using the same feature set.

In [72]:
#pip install xgboost
In [73]:
import xgboost as xgb

# XGBoost needs explicit categorical encoding or one-hot, unless using enable_categorical
X_train_xgb = X_train.copy()
X_test_xgb = X_test.copy()

model_xgb = xgb.XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=1000,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=6,
    min_child_weight=5,
    subsample=0.8,
    colsample_bytree=0.9,
    enable_categorical=True,
    early_stopping_rounds=50,
    eval_metric='mae'
)

model_xgb.fit(X_train_xgb, y_train, eval_set=[(X_test_xgb, y_test)], verbose=100)
preds_xgb = model_xgb.predict(X_test_xgb)
print(f"XGBoost MAE: {mean_absolute_error(y_test, preds_xgb):.4f}")

Per-Lot Model: Prophet¶

Benchmark against a classical per-lot seasonal decomposition approach, using final_df directly (no lag features needed — Prophet models temporal structure internally). Same train/test cutoff as the pooled model for a fair comparison.

from prophet import Prophet
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error
import numpy as np

results = {}

for lot, df_lot in lot_dfs.items():
    train = df_lot[df_lot['ds'] < cutoff_start]
    test = df_lot[df_lot['ds'] >= cutoff_start]

    if len(train) < 50 or len(test) < 10:   # skip lots with too little data either side
        continue

    m = Prophet(
        daily_seasonality=True,
        weekly_seasonality=True,
        yearly_seasonality=False,   # only ~2.5 months of data, not enough for yearly patterns
        changepoint_prior_scale=0.05  # default; controls trend flexibility — lower = more conservative
    )
    m.fit(train)

    forecast = m.predict(test[['ds']])
    preds = forecast['yhat'].clip(0, 1).values  # clip to valid occupancy rate range

    mae = mean_absolute_error(test['y'], preds)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test['y'], preds))
    results[lot] = {'mae': mae, 'rmse': rmse, 'n_test': len(test)}

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).T.sort_values('mae')
print(results_df)
print(results_df[['mae', 'rmse']].mean())

Prophet performs substantially worse than pooled LightGBM (MAE 0.076 vs. 0.021) — roughly 3–4x worse, and even worse than the naive baseline for several lots. With only ~2 months of history per lot, there isn't enough data for Prophet's seasonal decomposition to reliably separate trend/weekly/daily components in isolation. The pooled ML approach, which borrows strength across all 28 lots simultaneously and leans on recent-lag information (a stronger short-horizon signal than "typical Tuesday" seasonality), is the clear winner. Given this gap, SARIMA — a more rigid classical alternative — isn't worth pursuing further.

LightGBM Hyperparameter Tuning¶

A small, deliberate sweep (not a full grid search) around the current LightGBM config, to check whether there's meaningful headroom before finalizing the model.

In [82]:
train_set = lgb.Dataset(
    X_train, label=y_train,
    categorical_feature=['SystemCodeNumber'],
    params={'feature_pre_filter': False}
)
test_set = lgb.Dataset(
    X_test, label=y_test,
    categorical_feature=['SystemCodeNumber'],
    reference=train_set
)

configs = {
    'baseline (current)': {
        'learning_rate': 0.05, 'num_leaves': 31, 'min_data_in_leaf': 50,
        'feature_fraction': 0.9, 'bagging_fraction': 0.8, 'bagging_freq': 5,
    },
    'smaller_leaves': {
        'learning_rate': 0.05, 'num_leaves': 15, 'min_data_in_leaf': 50,
        'feature_fraction': 0.9, 'bagging_fraction': 0.8, 'bagging_freq': 5,
    },
    'more_leaves': {
        'learning_rate': 0.05, 'num_leaves': 63, 'min_data_in_leaf': 30,
        'feature_fraction': 0.9, 'bagging_fraction': 0.8, 'bagging_freq': 5,
    },
    'slower_lr': {
        'learning_rate': 0.02, 'num_leaves': 31, 'min_data_in_leaf': 50,
        'feature_fraction': 0.9, 'bagging_fraction': 0.8, 'bagging_freq': 5,
    },
    'less_regularized': {
        'learning_rate': 0.05, 'num_leaves': 31, 'min_data_in_leaf': 20,
        'feature_fraction': 1.0, 'bagging_fraction': 1.0, 'bagging_freq': 0,
    },
}

tuning_results = {}

for name, cfg in configs.items():
    params = {'objective': 'regression', 'metric': 'mae', 'verbose': -1, **cfg}
    m = lgb.train(
        params, train_set, num_boost_round=2000,
        valid_sets=[test_set],
        callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(stopping_rounds=50, verbose=False)]
    )
    preds = m.predict(X_test, num_iteration=m.best_iteration)
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, preds)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, preds))
    tuning_results[name] = {'mae': mae, 'rmse': rmse, 'best_iter': m.best_iteration}

print(pd.DataFrame(tuning_results).T.sort_values('mae'))

The final pooled LightGBM model was evaluated on the held-out test set (Dec 5–18, 2016) across five dimensions: per-lot accuracy, temporal accuracy, sensitivity to imputed data, residual bias, and error distribution.

Per-lot error. Mean absolute error ranged from 0.009 (NIA Car Parks) to 0.038 (BHMBRCBRG01) across the 28 lots — roughly a 4x spread. The worst-performing lots (BHMBRCBRG01, BHMBCCTHL01, BHMBRCBRG02) are the same lots flagged earlier in preprocessing for capacity-overshoot issues, suggesting their underlying occupancy dynamics are genuinely noisier or less consistent, not just harder for the model to learn. The best-performing lots (NIA Car Parks, Others-CCCPS202, NIA South) had errors below 0.015, indicating the model performs very well for the majority of lots even though a handful drag up the overall average.

Error by hour. Error is lowest during the stable midday period (11:00–15:00, MAE ~0.011–0.015) and highest at the operating-hours boundaries — 8:00 (0.051) and 16:00 (0.038). This is expected: these are the transition points where occupancy is rising or falling most steeply, so a lag-based model has the least reliable recent signal to extrapolate from. Predictions should be treated with more caution near opening and closing.

Error by day of week. Weekday error (Mon–Fri: 0.015–0.022) is generally lower than weekend error (Sat: 0.027, Sun: 0.023), though the spread is modest. This suggests weekday demand patterns are somewhat more regular/predictable than weekend patterns, consistent with the higher raw missingness observed in weekend data during preprocessing.

Imputed vs. observed rows. Rows that were originally missing and filled via interpolation show slightly higher error (MAE 0.024) than genuinely observed rows (MAE 0.020). The gap is small, indicating the model isn't being propped up by "easy" interpolated values, but it's a reasonable caveat: a small share of test performance is measured against synthetic rather than real data.

Residual bias (predicted vs. actual). The scatter plot shows predictions tracking the actual occupancy rate closely across the full 0–1 range, with points clustering tightly along the diagonal. A small number of outliers appear at low actual occupancy with high predicted occupancy (and vice versa), but there is no systematic directional bias — the model does not consistently over- or under-predict at any particular occupancy level.

Error distribution. Residuals (actual − predicted) are centered near zero (mean 0.0026, median 0.0024) with a standard deviation of 0.037, confirming the model is essentially unbiased on average. The distribution is sharply peaked but has a longer right tail (max residual 0.53) than left (min −0.31), meaning under-prediction of occupancy (real occupancy higher than forecast) is the rarer but more severe failure mode when it occurs — worth noting for any downstream use where under-forecasting capacity is more costly than over-forecasting it.

Time series inspection. A close look at the worst-performing lot (BHMBRCBRG01) shows the model tracks the daily rise-fall occupancy cycle well overall, correctly capturing the shape and timing of peaks. The main recurring miss is a slight lag/smoothing effect on the descending (evening) leg of each cycle — the model tends to predict a slower decline than actually occurs, consistent with the hour-16 error spike noted above.

Summary. The model shows strong, largely unbiased performance (MAE 0.021 pooled, well below the 0.048 naive baseline), with identifiable and explainable weak points: a few structurally noisier lots, the two operating-hour boundary periods, and a mild tendency to lag behind rapid evening declines. These are reasonable limitations for a lag-feature-based short-horizon forecaster and do not indicate a fundamental flaw in the modeling approach.

Summary & Limitations¶

  • Best model: pooled LightGBM, MAE 0.021 (vs. 0.048 naive baseline)
  • Excluded: 2 lots with poor data coverage (NIA North, BHMBRTARC01); rows with gaps longer than 2 hours (7.5% of resampled data)
  • Known weak points: a handful of structurally noisier lots (capacity-overshoot lots), the two operating-hour boundaries (8am/4pm), and a mild lag effect on rapid evening occupancy declines
  • Scope: short-horizon (30-min-ahead) forecasting during business hours (8am–4pm) only; not validated for multi-step or overnight forecasting
